One-page synthesis

Core thesis: During 20 three-monthly Abo-BTX A injections over five years, disease-specific and general quality-of-life measures showed early/intermediate improvements but many measures worsened late; the authors emphasize sustained improvement only in the SF-36 general-health domain, no meaningful CES-D improvement, and no clinically observed resistance.

The study followed 74 adults with hemifacial spasm (56 women, 18 men; mean age 60.8±7.5 years) who had already received a mean 10.85±5.95 prior Abo-BTX injections. Treatment was 100 U per session, delivered as 25 U at each of four ipsilateral orbicularis oculi/oris sites every three months for 20 injections. HFS30, AIMS, SF-36, and CES-D were repeatedly measured and analyzed with repeated-measures general linear models using sequential three-month visits and annual averages.

The source reports statistically significant longitudinal patterns for HFS30, AIMS, overall SF-36, and selected SF-36 domains, with late deterioration in several general-health domains. CES-D showed no significant improvement (sequential p=0.924; annual p=0.191). The strongest interpretive constraint is design: without a control group and with substantial pre-enrollment Abo-BTX exposure, observed trajectories cannot be attributed cleanly to treatment. Visit-specific denominators/attrition are not reported, multiplicity adjustment is not described, and portions of the reporting contain label ambiguity.

Load-bearing reporting issue: the Results text on page 2 states that after 45 months “HFS 30” increased to 15.9±2.3 (p=0.008) immediately after an AIMS result. The value/figure context appears AIMS-like, but this appraisal does not silently correct the source.

Methods and clinical question

PICO

P: Adults aged 18–80 years with hemifacial spasm able to provide reliable Thai HRQoL responses; analyzed n=74.
I: Abo-BTX A 100 U/session intramuscularly (25 U × 4 ipsilateral facial sites), every 3 months, 20 sessions over 5 years.
C: None.
O: HFS30, AIMS, and SF-36 change from baseline (primary); CES-D change (secondary).

Population and eligibility

Participants were 20–75 years old (mean±SD 60.8±7.5), with symptom duration 5.27±3.76 years. They were not treatment-naïve: the mean number of previous Abo-BTX injections was 10.85±5.95. Exclusions included lack of consent, potentially pregnant/lactating status under specified conditions, significant conditions judged likely to influence evaluation, and allergy to botulinum toxin A.

Intervention

A 500-U vial was diluted in 1.5 mL normal saline (approximately 333.33 U/mL) and used within two hours. Each session delivered 100 U intramuscularly with a 29G insulin needle at four sites: upper and lower outer orbicularis oculi and upper and lower outer orbicularis oris.

Measures and statistics

HFS30 assessed disease-specific quality of life; AIMS assessed abnormal involuntary movement; SF-36 provided eight general-health domains; CES-D assessed depressive symptoms. Measures were collected at baseline and before subsequent injections/visits. Repeated-measures general linear models evaluated three-month data and annual averages, considering linear, quadratic, and cubic models; tests were two-tailed at α=0.05.

The source does not report a multiplicity-control procedure, visit-specific analysis denominators, a formal resistance definition/assay, or a dedicated prospective adverse-event ascertainment framework.

Results

Disease-specific HRQoL and AIMS

HFS30 was reported as 30.1±2.3 at baseline, improving to 25.9±2.1 at 9 months and later 29.0±2.2 at 45 months; at 48 months it was reported as 39.2±4.4 (p=0.004). AIMS showed no significant change during the first 15 months (p=0.305), then was reported as 14.2±1.0 at 18 months and 11.2±0.9 at 42 months (p=0.041). The separate 45-month “HFS 30” value of 15.9±2.3 (p=0.008) is preserved as a source inconsistency rather than reclassified.

Annualized Figure 2 analyses report linear-model p=0.0001 for HFS30 and p=0.008 for AIMS. These p values show within-cohort temporal patterning, not a treatment-versus-control effect.

SF-36

Overall SF-36 was reported as 57.4±2.4 at baseline, reaching 61.3±3.0 at 27 months, then declining to 52.1±4.2 at 54 months (p=0.002). The annual general-health domain was reported as 45.8±1.5 in year 1 and 50±4.6 in year 5 (p=0.02). Physical functioning improved early from 61.4±3.6 at baseline to 67.8±4.2 at 9 months, but later fell to 50±6.2 at 57 months (p=0.001).

Sequential analyses reported no significant change in social functioning, bodily pain, mental health, or vitality (p=0.569, 0.948, 0.137, 0.322). Role-emotional was reported to decline to 45.1±9.3 at 57 months (quadratic p=0.013). Annual Figure 4 results similarly emphasize late worsening in several domains while general health improved, but the caption contains ambiguous panel labels.

CES-D and clinical resistance

CES-D showed no significant reduction across sequential visits (p=0.924) or annualized analyses (p=0.191); the paper states that no patients were treated with antidepressant medication. The authors report no observed clinical resistance during the study, but no neutralizing-antibody assay or operational resistance definition was used.

Appraisal: Annual averaging reduces visit-level detail and does not address the lack of a comparator group.

Figure 3 — Sequential SF-36 subdomains

Source locator: Page 4. Purpose/structure: Eight SF-36 domains are displayed. Physical functioning improved early (baseline 61.4±3.6; 67.8±4.2 at 9 months) but later fell to 50±6.2 at 57 months (p=0.001). Role-emotional declined to 45.1±9.3 at 57 months (quadratic p=0.013). General health and role-physical were borderline in the caption (p=0.06 each), while social functioning, bodily pain, mental health, and vitality were not significant in the sequential analyses.

Appraisal: Multiple domain-by-time analyses increase multiplicity concerns; the paper does not describe multiplicity adjustment.

Figure 4 — Annualized SF-36 subdomains

Source locator: Page 5. Purpose/structure: The caption reports general health improving across five years (p=0.02), while three other panels worsen in years 4–5 (p=0.04, p=0.03, p=0.03). Social functioning, bodily pain, mental health, and vitality are reported as non-significant (p=0.56, 0.94, 1.00, 0.56).

Appraisal: The source caption contains overlapping/ambiguous panel labels (“physical health” and “physical functioning” both described as top-middle). This appraisal preserves that ambiguity rather than silently relabeling the panels.

Figure 5 — Abo-BTX A injection sites

Source locator: Page 7. Purpose/structure: Injection diagram marks four ipsilateral sites: upper/lower outer orbicularis oculi and upper/lower outer orbicularis oris. The source states 25 U Abo-BTX A per site, for 100 U total per session, administered intramuscularly with a 29G insulin needle.

Appraisal: The regimen is reproducibly described, but this single-arm study does not establish comparative dose or injection-pattern superiority.

Discussion and conclusions

Authors’ interpretation

The authors interpret repeated Abo-BTX A as improving long-term disease-specific quality of life without serious complications and argue that general-health quality of life improves during early years but deteriorates across several domains by year five. They highlight sustained general-health-domain improvement and lack of observed clinical resistance.

They propose that neutralizing antibodies could contribute to diminished effects and should be examined in future work. This is a hypothesis raised by the authors; the present study did not measure antibodies and therefore does not establish that mechanism.

Independent appraisal of interpretation

The five-year duration, repeated standardized instruments, and explicit treatment regimen are genuine strengths. However, the design cannot distinguish treatment effects from natural history, aging, expectation, repeated-measure effects, regression to the mean, or changes in comorbidity. Prior exposure before baseline further complicates interpretation of “improvement from baseline.”

The article’s late deterioration signal is potentially useful for hypothesis generation, but incomplete retention reporting, multiple comparisons, absence of comparative treatment, and internal label ambiguity substantially limit causal or practice-changing conclusions.

Evaluation and appraisal

Verdict: Skim deeply. Best use is as a long-term descriptive signal and a design reference for future controlled longitudinal HFS studies. Do not use it alone to choose among botulinum toxins, compare Abo-BTX with microvascular decompression, quantify safety risk, or attribute waning effect to neutralizing antibodies.
Relevance
7/10

Long-term Abo-BTX treatment and quality-of-life outcomes in hemifacial spasm are clinically relevant, although the question is narrow.

Evidence basis: Five-year disease-specific, SF-36, movement, and depression trajectories in 74 adults.
Principal limit: Single condition, single intervention, QoL-centered outcomes.
Would raise score: Higher if paired with comparative long-term treatment or safety outcomes.

Novelty
6/10

Five-year repeated QoL follow-up is useful longitudinal evidence, but the study does not provide a comparative or mechanistic test.

Evidence basis: Twenty planned injections over five years with serial patient-reported measures.
Principal limit: No comparator; prior BTX exposure before enrollment.
Would raise score: Higher with controlled longitudinal data, antibody testing, or novel mechanistic validation.

Method strength
4/10

Prospective repeated measurement and standardized instruments are strengths, but causal inference is weak.

Evidence basis: Prespecified repeated-measures GLM, three-month assessments, explicit regimen and eligibility.
Principal limit: Single-arm design, prior-treated cohort, unclear visit-specific attrition, no multiplicity correction reported.
Would raise score: Higher with comparator/randomization, retention accounting, multiplicity strategy, and prespecified analysis plan.

Evidence strength
4/10

The source provides repeated quantitative trajectories but relies heavily on p values and has source-label inconsistencies.

Evidence basis: Reported mean±SE trajectories and annual/sequential models across multiple instruments.
Principal limit: No effect-size/CI framework, many repeated tests, no denominator by visit, ambiguous labels in parts of Results/Figure 4.
Would raise score: Higher with complete denominators, confidence intervals, corrected multiple testing, and internally reconciled reporting.

External validity
4/10

Findings may not generalize broadly beyond similar previously treated Thai adults with HFS.

Evidence basis: n=74, age 20–75 years, mostly women, one hospital-based cohort.
Principal limit: Single setting; restricted eligibility; mean 10.85 prior Abo-BTX injections.
Would raise score: Higher with multicenter enrollment, broader populations, and treatment-naïve strata.

Implementation value
4/10

The injection regimen is explicit, but the evidence is insufficient for a treatment-selection or dosing change.

Evidence basis: 100 U/session, 25 U at four ipsilateral orbicularis sites every three months, 20 sessions.
Principal limit: No comparative regimen, dedicated adverse-event rates, antibody testing, or treatment-alternative analysis.
Would raise score: Higher with comparative effectiveness, safety ascertainment, and dose-response data.

Main strengths: five-year prospective follow-up; repeated disease-specific and general QoL instruments; transparent injection regimen; both visit-level and annualized trajectories; explicit ethical/funding declarations.
Main limitations: no comparator; substantial prior Abo-BTX exposure; unclear visit-specific denominators/attrition; no multiplicity adjustment described; no formal antibody/resistance testing; no dedicated adverse-event incidence data; reporting inconsistencies in Results/Figure 4.

Confidence in appraisal: High for what this source reports and for the identified design/reporting limitations, because the full evaluated PDF and all main-text figures were reconciled. Moderate for the clinical meaning of late QoL deterioration, because the study design cannot isolate its cause.

Practice / implementation takeaways

Use now?No practice change from this study alone. It is descriptive longitudinal evidence, not comparative effectiveness evidence.
Monitoring insightLong-term HFS management may warrant attention to broader QoL domains rather than assuming sustained early gains across all domains.
Research designFuture studies should include comparator groups, treatment-naïve strata, explicit retention denominators, confidence intervals/effect sizes, multiplicity control, and prespecified resistance definitions.
Resistance questionNeutralizing-antibody testing is a proposed future question, not a finding of this study.
